summary: TRILL provides least-cost forwarding in networks of arbitrary topology without configuration. This document specifies ESADI, a protocol that lets TRILL switches share end station address information, optionally on a per-VLAN or per-fine-grained-label basis.

plainLanguage.summary: In a big mall, a directory tells you which shop is where. This RFC describes how special switches can share a directory of which computer sits behind which switch.

questions: how does trill learn mac addresses
what is the esadi confidence value
how does esadi elect a drb
subtitle: An optional protocol that lets TRILL switches share end station MAC addresses per VLAN or fine-grained label.

tldr.problem: TRILL switches normally learn end station addresses by watching data traffic, which is easy to spoof and slow to update when a station moves.
tldr.mechanism: ESADI runs a modified IS-IS reliable flooding instance per Data Label (VLAN or fine-grained label). Participating switches flood MAC-Reachability TLVs, each with a Confidence rating, as TRILL-encapsulated PDUs.
tldr.outcome: Addresses can come from authenticated enrollment, be protected by authenticated PDUs, and update quickly. The document updates RFC 6325 and its ESADI-LSP format is not backwards compatible.

today: RFC 7357 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6325, replacing its ESADI description, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the PDUs defined in RFC 7356.

sections.title: Why ESADI Exists
sections.content:
TRILL forwards frames over multi-hop networks with arbitrary topologies. A TRILL switch (also called an RBridge) can learn end station addresses in five ways, and by default it learns them from the data plane when frames enter and leave. ESADI (End Station Address Distribution Information) is the optional way for switches to tell each other about end station addresses and their TRILL switch of attachment.

The RFC lists two advantages over data plane learning. For security, ESADI can announce stations with an authenticated enrollment (for example EAP via 802.1X) and supports cryptographic authentication of its payloads. For speed, it gives fast updates: if a station moves, frames can otherwise be black-holed to the old egress switch until a remote cache times out, possibly for tens of seconds.

This document replaces the ESADI description in RFC 6325 and prevails where they conflict. It changes the ESADI-LSP format in a way that is not backwards compatible, justified by the very limited, if any, deployment of RFC 6325 ESADI.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually switches figure out where computers are by watching traffic, like guessing from footsteps. ESADI lets them just tell each other directly, and faster.

sections.title: How ESADI Works
sections.content:
ESADI is separate from the mandatory TRILL IS-IS. There is one ESADI instance per Data Label (a VLAN or a fine-grained label), each a modified instance of IS-IS reliable flooding. An RBridge announcing participation is an ESADI RBridge. Participation is announced by setting a flag bit in the Interested VLANs or Interested Labels sub-TLV from RFC 7176.

ESADI does no routing calculation, so it has no pseudonodes and no Hello PDUs. Its LSP, CSNP and PSNP payloads are formatted as Extended Level 1 Circuit Scope PDUs from RFC 7356, which allows up to 2**16 fragments. Neighbors are found by looking in the TRILL IS-IS link state database for RBridges that are data reachable and announce ESADI for that Data Label.

ESADI packets are sent as if they were TRILL Data packets. To each ESADI instance, every other participant looks like it sits on one multi-access virtual link. RBridges not running ESADI for that label do not decapsulate the packet, so ESADI is tunneled transparently through them. The inner Ethernet header uses the All-Egress-RBridges address, the Data Label, and the L2-IS-IS Ethertype.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches that care about a particular neighborhood join a private group chat for it. Switches outside the chat just pass the messages along without reading them.

sections.title: ESADI Packet Contents
sections.content:
An ESADI-LSP currently holds zero or more MAC-Reachability TLVs, optionally an Authentication TLV, and exactly one ESADI parameter APPsub-TLV. TLVs and sub-TLVs the instance does not understand are ignored. Because the PDUs are E-L1CS PDUs, Type and Length fields are 16 bits.

The primary information is the MAC-Reachability TLV from RFC 6165: unicast MAC addresses of end stations on a port and VLAN where the originating RBridge is Appointed Forwarder, each with a 1-octet Confidence value in the range 0 to 254. A received Confidence of 255 is treated as 254, so that statically configured local information with Confidence 255 can still override it. An RBridge may advertise all, some, or none of its local addresses.

The ESADI Parameter APPsub-TLV must be in ESADI-LSP number zero. It carries a 7-bit Priority (default 0x40) for DRB election, a CSNP Time in seconds (default 30), and a flags byte whose UN flag says the sender accepts unicast ESADI PDUs. ESADI-LSPs and their TLVs MUST NOT contain a Data Label ID; the Data Label comes from the enclosing TRILL Data packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is a list of computer addresses with a score for how sure the sender is. A header note says how important this switch is and how often it checks the list.

sections.title: Flooding, DRB and Unicast
sections.content:
Even though no pseudonode exists, a Designated RBridge (DRB) is still elected on the ESADI virtual link to send ESADI-CSNPs and answer ESADI-PSNPs. Candidates are the local instance and remote instances that are data reachable and announce ESADI for the label. The highest 7-bit priority wins, with ties broken by the larger System ID.

Reliable flooding follows IS-IS with changes for the multi-hop setting. A new neighbor triggers sending of self-originated ESADI-LSP fragments, and instances SHOULD wait a bit first to avoid a surge. The RFC suggests a random value based on the nickname, such as 2000 * nickname / 2**16 milliseconds. Non-originators delay and jitter their responses to CSNP and PSNP requests so that the originator has time to respond first. Because multi-hop tree distribution is less reliable than one local hop, a non-DRB that sees neighbors SHOULD also send an ESADI-CSNP if none has been seen or sent for the average of the DRB's CSNP Time and its own.

Multicasting on a virtual link of multi-hop trees can cost more than unicast, so ESADI PDUs MAY be TRILL unicast to a switch that advertises support through the UN flag. The M bit is then zero and the egress nickname is the destination. The priority bit from RFC 7356 SHOULD be set on ESADI-LSP fragment zero and SHOULD NOT be set on other fragments.

The payload size is limited: the inner ESADI payload MUST NOT exceed Sz minus 24 for a VLAN instance or Sz minus 28 for a fine-grained label instance. For fragment zero, the payload MUST NOT exceed 1446 bytes (VLAN) or 1442 bytes (FGL).
sections.plainLanguage: One switch in each group is picked as the helper who regularly reads out a summary so nobody misses anything. Switches wait a random moment before talking, so they do not all shout at the newcomer at once.

sections.title: End Station Address Handling
sections.content:
A TRILL campus manager can use Confidence to let some learning sources prevail over others. Address information from a registration protocol such as 802.1X with a cryptographic EAP method may be more reliable than information seen in data traffic, so it could be announced via ESADI with high Confidence.

Learned addresses are forgotten through changes in ESADI-LSPs; the originating RBridge decides when to remove them. A switch that stops participating clears the ESADI Participation bit and sends a final ESADI-LSP nulling out its information.

With ESADI, the same MAC address in one Data Label can persistently appear reachable via two or more RBridges. This document replaces a sentence of RFC 6325 section 4.2.6. When Confidences are tied, the ingress RBridge MUST either (1) pseudorandomly choose one least-cost egress and send all traffic for that MAC and label to it, for example using FNV-32 over its own nickname, the MAC, the label and the candidate nicknames, mod k, or (2) if it supports ECMP and will not be disturbed by return traffic from several RBridges, MAY use flow-level ECMP.
sections.plainLanguage: If two switches both claim the same computer, the sender picks one at random and sticks with it, so the answer does not keep flipping back and forth.

sections.title: Authentication and Privacy
sections.content:
ESADI PDUs can carry an Authentication TLV. By default, if TRILL IS-IS LSP authentication is in effect, ESADI uses the same algorithm, with keying material derived as HMAC-SHA256 ("TRILL ESADI", IS-IS-LSP-shared-key). If IS-IS LSP authentication is not in effect, ESADI PDUs are by default unsecured too. Operators MAY configure other keying material.

Combined with authenticated registration, ESADI reachability can be much more trustworthy than data plane learning, but it still means trusting all RBridges holding the keying material. ESADI also makes multiple attachments of one MAC address explicitly and persistently visible, which data plane learning would not.

The RFC also warns about privacy. MAC addresses of user end stations can identify users, so reachability data is sensitive. Operators should balance this against the value of short attachment histories and SHOULD NOT keep logs of MAC reachability longer than clearly required (the text says they should not maintain them longer than clearly required).
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can be sealed with a secret handshake so only trusted switches can speak. Because the lists show who is where, they should not be kept longer than needed.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created two flag-bit sub-registries, "Interested VLANs Flag Bits" and "Interested Labels Flag Bits". Both assign bit 3 as the ES (ESADI Participation) bit, which when set means the originating RBridge participates in ESADI for the indicated Data Labels.

IANA also allocated IS-IS Application Identifier 1 under the Generic Information TLV (#251) for TRILL and created a sub-registry of TRILL APPsub-TLV types. Type 1 is ESADI-PARAM; types 0, 255 and 65535 are reserved, and other types are available by IETF Review. TRILL APPsub-TLVs MUST NOT alter basic IS-IS operation such as adjacency establishment, the update process or the decision process.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number lists now have a spot saying "this switch is in the group" and a spot for the settings message.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 6325
sections.content: Appendix A summarizes interoperability. The ESADI-LSP format change is not backwards compatible. Unicast ESADI support is backwards compatible because it is used only when the recipient signals support. The new staggered timing of non-originator responses and of new-neighbor sends affects only congestion. Handling of duplicate MAC reachability is substantially modified, but a mixture of implementations conforming to RFC 6325 and to this document causes no problem; the more that follow the new behavior, the better the traffic spreading and the less address flip-flopping.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the old rules were swapped for better ones. The message layout changed so old and new do not talk to each other, but the other changes are safe to mix.

layers.label: Data Label
layers.detail: The VLAN or FGL of interest

layers.label: ESADI Payload
layers.detail: E-L1CS style LSP, CSNP or PSNP

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Minimum of 3; unsigned, network byte order.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; sent as zero, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Priority
fields.desc: DRB priority for the ESADI instance; default 0x40.

fields.name: CSNP Time
fields.desc: Seconds in which the DRB sends at least three ESADI-CSNPs; default 30.
